newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian government reviewing Iran credit.
newsitem.headline: Australian government reviewing Iran credit.

text.p: Australia's foreign minister said on Tuesday cabinet would discuss the future of a A$950 million (US$737 million) line of credit to Iran after a German court linked the Islamic state to terrorism.

Foreign Minister Alexander Downer told reporters before a cabinet meeting that Canberra's response to the court decision would be discussed. Australia has already withdrawn its ambassador to Iran for consultations.
Entering the meeting, Downer was asked if the credit facility to Iran was "on the line".
"That's an issue we've been discussing with the Iranians for quite some time," Downer said.
"Beyond that, I'm not going to get into speculation about different things we could do because I think it's important there's a reasonably well-coordinated international approach to the issue."
Australia recalled its ambassador to Iran, Stuart Hume, after a German court last week ruled Tehran had ordered the 1992 murders of Kurdish activists in Berlin.

Downer has said Australia would consider a further response after studying the detail of the court ruling and consulting other governments, including European Union countries, Canada and the United States.
Australia is still awaiting details of the court verdict.
The Labor opposition has demanded a halt to all trade with Iran, which is the biggest market for Australian wheat.
Two-way trade is heavily in Australia's favour -- A$650 million in Australian exports and A$28 million in imports from Iran in calendar 1996.
Most Australian exports came in the form of wheat sales, valued at more than A$500 million. Wheat farmers have appealed to the government not to endanger trade ties.
The court said Iran's political leadership ordered the killings of a group of Iranian Kurdish leaders in Berlin's Mykonos restaurant in 1992.

It avoided names but said the assassination was ordered by a secret special operations committee whose members included Iran's president, religious leader, intelligence minister and head of foreign policy. Tehran denies supporting terrorism.
